messages.author: f13fe7e880ed6103
messages.subject: Chopin and Ridgway [2015]
parts:
Has anyone looked at the experiments in Chopin and Ridgway [2015]
(http://arxiv.org/abs/1506.08640)? They compare a bunch of sampling
methods (including HMC/NUTS as implemented in Stan) on some benchmark
logistic regression datasets. I'm particularly wondering what's going
on with Figure 5.5, where Metropolis-Hastings has consistently better
ESS for fixed CPU time than HMC/NUTS. We read it in reading group
today and the best guess was that they use a proposal distribution in
which the covariance comes from first running EP, and that's why MH is
doing so well.

The authors mention that you can do this to initialize the mass matrix
in HMC (has anyone tried this?) but I think they just ran Stan with
defaults so presumably the mass matrix is diagonal in the experiments
they report...

Seth

OK, might be worth chatting with the authors; I'm not sure what stage
the paper is in but the version I read seemed to be a draft. Seeing as
they didn't discuss this result one way or another (other than to
mention the surprisingly good performance of MH) they're probably not
sure why HMC didn't work better. Anyone know Chopin and want to email
him? Otherwise I'm happy to, as it seems worth figuring this out.

messages.author: a236d3d356ca53fd
messages.subject: Re: [stan-dev] Chopin and Ridgway [2015]
parts:
I don't think the experiments they have are very useful for MCMC method comparisons, since they use fixed prior for weights beta and they are sampling only beta. This is quite easy posterior although Cauchy prior may cause fat tail with known problems. For IS and MH they use EP approximation as the proposal, which works well as they don't have other unknowns than beta. There is not yet working "black box" EP, and EP can be used only for a restricted model structures (e.g. unknown hierarchical prior scales and unknown likelihood scales are easy). We have seen that for *some models* ADVI+IS works well, and it might be possible that ADVI+MH would work well also *for some models*.

Aki

Right, almost all of the logistic regression with data out of the UCI database
are pretty Gaussian and hence easy to fit. But that’s also one of the biggest
points of the paper — these models are way too easy to be a useful benchmark.
